title: Embrace Opportunities and Face Challenges: Using ChatGPT in Undergraduate Students' Collaborative Interdisciplinary Learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using ChatGPT can support collaborative interdisciplinary learning in higher education, specifically among undergraduate students working on digital literacy topics. The authors note that empirical evidence on ChatGPT's educational impact was limited at the time, especially for collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving. Although the retrieval topic concerns causal evidence for foundational reading outcomes in K-12, this study does not address K-12 reading and should be treated only as adjacent evidence on classroom use of generative AI, not evidence for reading instruction outcomes.

The study used a two-week quasi-experimental classroom implementation in which 130 first- and second-year undergraduates in a digital literacy course completed group activities on AI and Blockchain either with or without ChatGPT support. Some groups used standard ChatGPT, while others used a "ChatGPT Persona" mode in which the system was assigned a disciplinary persona to act like an additional teammate. Students worked in face-to-face collaborative groups using Miro in a flipped-classroom format, and the researchers collected weekly self-report surveys on collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving, physical engagement, and cognitive engagement, along with written reflections about ChatGPT use.

Participants were undergraduate students at a single public university in Singapore, drawn from STEM and non-STEM programs. The setting was an in-class university course rather than a K-12 or school-supported literacy setting. Outcomes were not academic achievement or reading measures; instead, they focused on perceived engagement and collaborative problem-solving. Quantitative analyses found significant main effects of topic, but no main effect of ChatGPT condition on the dependent variables. There was a significant interaction between disciplinary background and ChatGPT condition for physical engagement and a marginal interaction for cognitive engagement, with non-STEM students reporting higher engagement in non-ChatGPT conditions.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT should not be applied uniformly; its usefulness depends on task design and learner background. Qualitative reflections showed perceived benefits such as efficiency, brainstorming support, filling knowledge gaps, and human-like responses, alongside concerns about inaccuracy, generic responses, overreliance, and reduced critical thinking. For the purposes of the retrieval question, this paper provides no direct causal evidence on generative AI for foundational reading outcomes in K-12 classrooms; it is adjacent higher-education evidence centered on collaborative learning and self-reported engagement rather than literacy achievement.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental study with some comparative structure, but it is outside K-12, not focused on reading, and relies primarily on self-reported engagement/problem-solving rather than direct academic achievement measures. The design lacks the strength and relevance required for strong causal evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: Impacts are mixed and unclear: there was no overall ChatGPT main effect on the primary measured outcomes, with only subgroup interactions and qualitative perceptions of benefit and harm. For the user's target domain of K-12 foundational reading, this study provides no direct impact evidence and only adjacent, indirect evidence from higher education collaborative learning.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a conversational peer agent in undergraduate small-group digital literacy activities on AI and blockchain, sometimes in a 'persona' mode to simulate an interdisciplinary teammate contributing ideas during collaborative problem-solving.

finding.finding_summary: In a two-week quasi-experimental study of 130 undergraduates, ChatGPT condition showed no overall main effect on physical or cognitive engagement, but there was a significant interaction with disciplinary background for physical engagement and a marginal interaction for cognitive engagement. Non-STEM students were more physically and cognitively engaged in the non-ChatGPT condition, while STEM students showed no significant engagement difference by condition; topic effects favored the AI module over the blockchain module (physical engagement F(1,202)=15.15, p<.001, η²=.06; cognitive engagement F(1,202)=5.91, p<.05, η²=.02).
finding.measure: Self-report Likert surveys of physical engagement and cognitive engagement completed after class activities
finding.effect_size: η²=.06 for physical engagement topic effect; η²=.02 for cognitive engagement topic effect; interaction η²=.03 for physical engagement and η²=.01 for cognitive engagement
finding.std_deviation: Reported descriptively by subgroup; e.g., AI physical engagement SDs ranged from 0.60 to 0.79 in ChatGPT groups and 0.63 to 0.72 in non-ChatGPT groups

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT did not produce a significant main effect on collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving in this quasi-experiment. Students' collaborative problem-solving ratings were instead significantly higher for the AI topic than for blockchain (F(1,202)=12.40, p<.01), with no significant condition effect and no meaningful interaction attributable to ChatGPT on this outcome.
finding.measure: Three-item self-report collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving scale adapted from the Team Collaboration Questionnaire
finding.effect_size: Topic effect η²=.05; ChatGPT condition effect not significant
finding.std_deviation: Reported descriptively by subgroup; e.g., collaborative problem-solving SDs ranged from 0.51 to 1.16 across AI subgroups and 0.59 to 0.71 across blockchain subgroups

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative reflections indicated that many students perceived ChatGPT as improving efficiency by quickly generating consolidated information and helping brainstorming, but these benefits were offset by concerns about inaccuracy, generic responses, repetition, and the need for fact-checking and additional probing. Because efficiency was not tested with an objective performance metric and no causal quantitative estimate was reported, the evidence for operational efficiency remains suggestive rather than established.
finding.measure: Post-activity written reflections coded into qualitative themes such as efficiency, idea generation, and need for verification
